This was the first time ever I installed a Linux distro, although I had been thinking about it for a while. I chose Mint because I saw people here on voat recommend it, after looking into it and some other distros, it seemed like the right choice: looks nice with Cinnamon, easy to use and install, good support forums, good functionality/compatibility. I used this guide (one of the first google results to "how to dual boot mint") to backup windows and dual boot, following the guide was easy. There is no way in hell that I could have installed Mint without that guide though (now I could). It was exciting and I learned quite a bit, since I usually don't do much on my computer other than game and browse:

I had to use my UEFI boot thingy for the first time ever to dual boot Mint and it didn't work at first, so I took a wild guess and installed a bios update first from my laptop manufacturer's website and that worked much to my surprise. Then I had to download the Mint .Iso and partition my hard drive which I had never done before. Also moved all my files (so music, pictures, videos and documents) to a separate hard drive partition. I turned off secure boot and extracted the Mint .Iso to a thumbdrive. Then I used the "boot from disk/thumbdrive" option in the windows 8 menu. Got Mint to run and installed it. I restarted immediately and almost had a heart attack when windows booted up straight away. Then I googled a bit and switched the boot order for GRUB to #1. After making sure everything worked, I deleted windows. From then on, using Mint has been smooth sailing and I feel like I have more control over my computer.

The biggest change for me, was using the software manager to install things, but that's not hard, it's like using Google play or Itunes, except only for free, non-bullshit stuff. After getting used to things, as a windows user, there wasn't anything that I was really missing on Mint other than some games (that I might still get to work with wine). There is a free linux program installed on Mint by default for almost everything you can do on windows:

  • Libre office instead of microsoft office. I was using libre office already anyway cause I'm a cheap fuck which was one of my main motivations for trying linux in the first place. If I ever get rich, I swear I will donate to all the FOSS stuff I use now, I think the idea is great.

  • Gimp instead of photoshop (I don't really know how to use either properly, I only have toddler-level paint skills). Blender is free and works for 3-d modelling

  • VLC media players instead of windows media player

  • Steam works no problem, as do 1600 games on it, but not all games do which might be a deal breaker for lots of people. Dota and csgo both work flawlessly which is really all I care about anyway, when it comes to games.

  • Firefox is installed on mint by default, so youtube,twitch etc. work, but I downloaded chrome instead because it let's you watch netflix as well which firefox and other linux browsers don't really support (yet). I now use firefox for browsing and chrome for netflix and flashgames.

Mint detects and installs drivers for your hardware automatically, so everything just worked for me. I did have to download nvidia drivers seperately which worked. The only issue I have now, is that I get screen tearing when watching netflix on chrome. There's a fix, but I've been too lazy to do it yet. No idea why, but sound quality on Mint is amazing, so that's a definite plus. Next I will try using wine to play starcraft and Unreal Tournament. I will try out some other distros (Arch for the 1337 bonus points), once I get bored of Mint.

In the wake of the prosecution and subsequent suicide of Aaron Swartz, lawmakers have proposed to amend the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Representative Zoe Lofgren has drafted a bill that would help "prevent what happened to Aaron from happening to other Internet users". Aaron's Law would exclude terms of service violations from the 1984 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and from the wire fraud statute, despite the fact that Swartz was not prosecuted based on Terms of Service violations.

In addition to Lofgren's efforts, Representatives Darrell Issa and Jared Polis (also on the House Judiciary Committee) raised questions about the government's handling of the case. Polis called the charges "ridiculous and trumped up," referring to Swartz as a "martyr." Issa, who also chairs the House Oversight Committee, announced an investigation of the Justice Department's prosecution.

As of May 2014, Aaron's Law was stalled in committee, reportedly due to tech company Oracle's financial interests.
